promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Stock forms and scales of production

questions.q: Which force is a pulling force that tends to stretch or lengthen a material?
questions.explain: Tension is a pulling force that acts to stretch or extend a material.

questions.q: Which force acts to twist a material, such as when wringing out a wet cloth?
questions.explain: Torsion is a twisting force applied along the length of a material.

questions.q: A wooden shelf carrying heavy books sags in the middle. Which forces act across its thickness?
options: Compression along the top surface and tension along the bottom surface
Tension along the top surface and compression along the bottom surface
Shear on both the top and bottom surfaces
Torsion along the entire length of the shelf
questions.explain: In bending, the upper surface is squeezed (compression) while the lower surface is stretched (tension).

questions.q: Which everyday action applies mainly a shear force to a material?
options: Cutting paper with a pair of scissors
Squashing a sponge in your hand
questions.explain: Scissors apply two opposing forces that slide past each other, producing a shear force that cuts the material.

questions.q: Why does laminating (bonding several thin layers together) make a material such as timber stronger and stiffer?
options: The layers spread and resist loads together, resisting bending better than a single sheet
It removes all moisture, making the material fully waterproof
It makes the material lighter by trapping air between layers
It allows the material to conduct heat away more quickly
questions.explain: Bonding thin layers combines their strengths so the laminate resists bending and other forces far better than a single layer.

questions.q: Which mechanical property describes a material's ability to be drawn out into a thin wire?
questions.explain: Ductility is the ability of a material to be drawn out into a wire without breaking.

questions.q: Which property is most important when selecting a material for the handle of a saucepan?
options: It should be a thermal insulator so the handle stays cool to hold
It should be a good thermal conductor to spread heat evenly
It should be highly ductile so it can be drawn into wire
It should be transparent so the food can be seen
questions.explain: A thermal insulator resists heat transfer, keeping the handle cool and safe to hold while cooking.

questions.q: A designer needs a material for a cycle safety helmet that absorbs impact energy without shattering. Which property should they prioritise?
questions.explain: Toughness is the ability to absorb impact energy and resist sudden fracture, which is essential for a protective helmet.

questions.q: Aluminium is extracted from which naturally occurring ore?
questions.explain: Aluminium is refined from bauxite ore, whereas haematite is an iron ore.

questions.q: Most polymers (plastics) are manufactured from which primary raw source?
questions.explain: Most polymers are made from crude oil, which is refined and processed into plastic materials.

questions.q: Hardwoods such as oak and mahogany are generally obtained from which type of tree?
questions.explain: Hardwoods come from broad-leaved deciduous trees, which are typically slower growing than softwood conifers.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the '6 Rs' of sustainable design?
questions.explain: The 6 Rs are Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Rethink and Repair, so 'Replace' is not one of them.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a Life Cycle Assessment (LCA)?
options: An evaluation of a product's environmental impact from raw material extraction through to disposal
A calculation of only the profit a product will make over its lifetime
A test of how long a product will last before it breaks
A survey of how many customers like the product's appearance
questions.explain: An LCA assesses environmental impact across the whole life of a product, from material sourcing to end-of-life disposal.

questions.q: A clothing brand wants to reduce the social footprint of its manufacturing. Which action best achieves this?
options: Ensuring workers are paid fairly and have safe working conditions
Increasing the speed of the production line to make more items
Switching to the cheapest available overseas labour
Using brighter synthetic dyes on the fabric
questions.explain: The social footprint concerns the impact on people, so fair pay and safe conditions directly improve it.

questions.q: Producing a single, unique bespoke item, such as a tailor-made suit, is an example of which scale of production?
questions.explain: One-off (job) production makes a single, individual product to a specific requirement.

questions.q: A factory assembles hundreds of thousands of identical smartphones on a production line. This is best described as?
questions.explain: Mass production makes very large numbers of identical products, usually on an assembly line.

questions.q: A bakery makes 500 loaves in the morning, then changes its equipment to make a run of bread rolls. Making a set quantity before switching product is an example of?
questions.explain: Batch production makes a specific quantity of one item before the equipment is changed over to make another.

questions.q: Anodising is a protective and decorative finishing process most commonly applied to which metal?
questions.explain: Anodising thickens the natural oxide layer on aluminium to protect it and allow it to be coloured.

questions.q: Galvanising protects steel from corrosion by coating it with a layer of which metal?
questions.explain: Galvanising coats steel with zinc, which corrodes in preference to the steel and prevents rusting.

questions.q: A metal coat hook is heated and then dipped into a fluidised bed of polymer powder to give it a smooth, durable plastic coating. This finishing process is called?
questions.explain: In dip coating, a heated metal part is dipped into fluidised polymer powder, which melts onto it to form a plastic coating.
